title: Credit Unions Versus Banks
summary: Compare two real candidates using the same evidence. Then deliver your verdict: bank, credit union or hybrid.
subtitle: A Bank and a Credit Union Walk Into a Comparison. Neither Has Brought the Fee Schedule.

blocks.text: Banks and credit unions can both offer everyday accounts, savings, loans and digital services.
Their ownership and rules differ, but the label on the door does not decide which bank or credit union fits your life, or what a product will cost you.

In this Member-Owned Debate, you are the judge. Bank counsel and credit-union counsel will present their strengths, then you will question two real candidates using the same evidence. Your verdict may be a bank, a credit union or a hybrid that uses both.
FCAC: Choosing a financial institution
The useful question is “Which bank or credit union, and which product, does the job I need?” The question “Which type is best?” has no good answer.

blocks.text: The Four Rules of This Debate

items.title: SAME CASE
items.text: Compare both candidates against the same needs, habits and evidence date.

items.title: ACTUAL TERMS
items.text: Use current fees, rates, features and who qualifies, not reputation or a friend’s old story.

items.title: LEGAL IDENTITY
items.text: Confirm if it is a bank, a federal credit union or a provincial one.

items.title: PROTECTION
items.text: Check the deposit insurer, the eligible product and the insured category. Confirm the coverage limit before you put money in.

items.title: “All banks are basically alike, and all credit unions are basically alike.”
items.text: Banks and credit unions can each differ in fees, rates, branch and ATM access, apps, products, who qualifies and service. Compare the real candidates, not two stereotypes wearing name tags.

blocks.text: Ownership does not decide who wins this case. Evidence does, and the evidence is coming up next.
blocks.detail: You are about to hear both sides make their case, then cross-examine them with your own numbers.
blocks.extra: Opening arguments are next, followed by six claims that need receipts.

sections.title: Opening Arguments: What Each Structure Can Offer

items.title: OPENING ARGUMENT 01 — Bank counsel — The case for scale
items.text: Often offers wide national or international access, plus big ATM and digital networks. It also offers many personal, business and investment services. Canadian banks are usually owned by shareholders. Federally regulated banks follow federal consumer rules that FCAC oversees. Key points: Broad access, Digital network, Service range. Judge’s question: Is the wider access and range worth the total cost for the way you bank?

items.title: OPENING ARGUMENT 02 — Credit-union counsel — The case for membership
items.text: A credit union is a co-operative owned by its members. Members may get a vote, and the credit union may focus on a community, region or group. Some credit unions are regulated by their province. Federal credit unions follow federal rules. Key points: Member-owned, Community focus, Voting rights. Judge’s question: Do membership and local service improve the product and access you need?

Cross-Examination: Six Claims That Need Receipts

items.title: ACCESS
items.text: Branches, own-network ATMs, travel and use abroad — Can I use it where I live, work and travel?

items.title: COST
items.text: Package fees, transaction limits, ATM fees, transfer fees and minimum balances — What is my total cost for a year?

items.title: TECH
items.text: App, alerts, mobile deposit, card controls and support — Do the tools fit my routine and my needs?

items.title: SERVICE
items.text: Local advice, hours, phone service and how to complain — What happens when an easy transaction gets complicated?

items.title: BORROWING
items.text: Who qualifies, the rate, the total cost and flexibility — Am I comparing written offers, not guesses?

items.title: RANGE
items.text: Personal, business, investment and international products — Do I need this range, or do I just like the brochure?

items.title: “Member-owned means a credit union will always charge less and provide better service.”
items.text: Member ownership changes who runs it, not the laws of arithmetic. A credit union may offer excellent value. Another may not fit where you live or how you bank. Compare the real fee schedule, service record and product terms.

blocks.text: Ownership tells you who runs it. It does not guarantee the lowest fee, best app, highest savings rate or warmest conversation about a forgotten password.
Meet Lucas
paragraphs: Lucas lives in Langley, BC. He travels for contract work and is saving for a reliable car. His national bank has wide ATM access and a strong app. A nearby credit union offers local advice and a lower-fee account. One friend calls banks “too corporate.” Another calls credit unions “small-town banking with Wi-Fi.” Lucas lets the evidence talk instead.

The credit union’s everyday account is cheaper, and its branch opens on Saturdays. The bank has more no-fee ATMs along his work routes and better card support abroad. Each one wins a different category.

A neighbour says membership should make Lucas’s car loan easier to get. Tempting, but a membership share is not a tiny golden ticket. Both places still check his credit, income and debt. Lucas asks for written terms instead of filing extra applications just to find out.

For a moment he wants to pick one and be done: one login, one branch, one app. But the scorecard keeps showing the same pattern. The bank wins on daily use and travel. The credit union wins on cost and Saturday hours. Choosing only one means paying for whichever weakness he ignores.
So he downloads both fee schedules, tests each app and maps the ATMs along his two work routes. He writes the date beside every answer.

Lucas keeps the bank for payroll, bills, travel and ATM access. He opens the credit union’s no-fee savings account for the car fund, after confirming it is BC-authorized and the deposit qualifies for CUDIC protection. Each account has one job and no extra fee riding along. Choosing where to bank, Lucas learns, is not a marriage ceremony. It is closer to hiring two contractors for two jobs.

blocks.text: Lucas’s scorecard turned a fuzzy gut feeling into a 7-point verdict he could defend.
blocks.detail: The same weighted scorecard that settled Lucas’s case can settle yours, criterion by criterion.
blocks.extra: Section 03 hands you the same scorecard, ready to fill in.

blocks.text: Give each criterion an importance weight from 1 (helpful) to 3 (essential). Rate each candidate from 1 (poor fit) to 5 (strong fit), using current evidence. Multiply weight × rating.
A high score guides the verdict. It does not excuse a failed safety requirement.
NON-NEGOTIABLE GATE
Before scoring, confirm four things: who it legally is, how to complain, who insures the deposits and whether you can get the product.
If one cannot be verified, pause that candidate. Safety is a pass/fail question, not five bonus points for a charming app.
Lucas’s Fictional Evidence Sheet

items.text: Weight: 3 — Bank: 4 × 3 = 12 — Credit union: 5 × 3 = 15

blocks.text: SCORE
Bank: 58 | Credit union: 51.
The bank is the stronger all-purpose fit for Lucas’s work and travel right now. The credit union may still earn one carefully chosen job if its benefit outweighs the extra account hassle.
Do Not Turn a Product Inquiry Into an Application

Ask who qualifies, sample rates, fees and required documents first. A borrowing rate can depend on you and the product. Membership or a brand name never guarantees approval. If you do need to apply, wait until you have narrowed your shortlist.

items.title: “Joining a credit union means I will automatically qualify for its loan or best advertised rate.”
items.text: Membership can let you apply, but the bank or credit union still reviews your application, and the advertised rate may come with conditions. Ask what affects whether you qualify, your rate and the total cost of borrowing.

blocks.text: A lower advertised borrowing rate is not a verdict. Compare who qualifies, term, payment, fees, early-payoff rules and total cost using the same amount and timeline.

sections.title: Deposit Protection: Verify the Institution, Product and Category

items.title: LAYER 1 — BANK OR FEDERAL CREDIT UNION
items.text: At a CDIC member, eligible deposits are protected up to $100,000 in each insured category. That includes principal and interest. Confirm membership, the product and the ownership category.

items.title: LAYER 2 — PROVINCIAL CREDIT UNION
items.text: The provincial insurer and its rules apply. Limits, covered deposits and categories can differ by province. A credit-union brand may also be federal instead.

items.title: LAYER 3 — PRODUCT
items.text: Chequing, savings and eligible term deposits may qualify. Mutual funds, stocks, bonds, exchange-traded funds and cryptocurrency are not CDIC-insured deposits just because you bought them at a member bank.

blocks.text: CDIC: What’s covered

items.title: “Everything sold inside an insured financial institution is deposit-insured.”
items.text: Deposit insurance protects eligible deposits only. Mutual funds, stocks, bonds, ETFs and cryptocurrency do not become insured deposits because of the building, app or adviser that sold them.

blocks.text: Deposit protection follows three things: the bank or credit union itself, the eligible product and the ownership category. It does not follow the colour of the logo. A familiar brand is a clue to investigate, not proof.

sections.title: Province Lens: The Map Changes the Protection Route

items.title: AB
items.text: Alberta CUDGC guarantees deposits, with interest, at Alberta credit unions. ATB deposits have a separate Alberta government guarantee.

items.title: BC
items.text: CUDIC protects eligible deposits at BC-authorized credit unions. A federal credit union uses CDIC instead.

items.title: ON
items.text: FSRA insures eligible non-registered deposits up to $250,000 at Ontario credit unions. Eligible registered deposits have no limit.

items.title: NB / PEI / NL
items.text: Provincial credit-union protection applies. Limits and categories differ. Check the bank or credit union and the product with NBCUDIC, PEI CUDIC or CUDGCNL.

blocks.text: Coverage rules can change. Check the official insurer again before you open, renew or add a lot to a deposit.

A hybrid looks useful.

blocks.text: Before You Deliver Your Verdict

items.title: “Once I choose a bank or credit union, loyalty means keeping every product there.”
items.text: Using one bank or credit union can make tracking simpler and may earn a discount, but another may fit a specific job better. A hybrid can work when its benefit outweighs the extra fees, transfers, passwords and checking.

blocks.text: Convenience has value, but putting everything in one place has trade-offs. FCAC recommends comparing consumer protection, fees, rates, access, service and complaints. Do not assume that one bank or several is automatically better.
FCAC: Choosing a financial institution

sections.title: Your Action (Fill Out Form): Member-Owned Debate

blocks.text: Use public product information and short names for each bank or credit union.
Do not record account numbers, passwords, PINs, card details, income documents or government ID numbers in course notes.
Member-Owned Debate Closing Checklist

items.title: The jobs are clear.
items.text: Every shortlisted account solves a stated need instead of just collecting features.

items.title: The evidence is current.
items.text: Fees, rates, access, who qualifies and service details share a recorded comparison date.

items.title: The scoring is fair.
items.text: Both candidates face the same criteria, weights and real-life usage pattern.

items.title: Protection is verified.
items.text: You checked an official source for who insures it, which product is covered, how it is owned and the limit.

items.title: The verdict is manageable.
items.text: A hybrid gives each account one job and sets rules for transfers, fees, checking and closing.

blocks.text: Compare specific banks and credit unions against the same needs.
blocks.detail: Check their legal status and deposit protection, then pick the simplest setup that fits you best overall.

blocks.text: The winner is not the one with the best category label. It is the one whose current, verified terms keep doing the assigned job after the promotion, first statement and first inconvenient Tuesday.

items.title: Bank
items.text: A deposit-taking business usually owned by shareholders. In Canada, federal law (the Bank Act) regulates banks.

items.title: Credit union
items.text: A co-operative that takes deposits and is owned by its own members.

items.title: Member-owner
items.text: A credit-union member who may hold a membership share and a vote, under the credit union’s rules.

items.title: Federal credit union
items.text: A member-owned credit union that follows the federal Bank Act.

items.title: Provincial credit union
items.text: A credit union set up and regulated under the laws of a province.

items.title: Deposit insurance
items.text: Protection for eligible deposits if a covered bank or credit union fails, within the insurer’s limits.

items.title: Eligible deposit
items.text: Money in a product that qualifies for deposit insurance under the rules that apply.

items.title: Insured category
items.text: An ownership type, such as a single or joint account, that gets its own deposit-insurance coverage.

items.title: Membership share
items.text: An amount you may need to pay to become a member-owner. It does not guarantee credit approval or a dividend.

items.title: Hybrid setup
items.text: Using more than one bank or credit union, with each account given one clear job.

questions: Which five things matter most when choosing a bank or credit union? Give each a weight from 1 (helpful) to 3 (essential).
Name the two you are comparing. Is each a bank, a federal credit union or a provincial credit union? Note the date of your evidence.
Rate each one from 1 to 5 on cost, access, apps, service and product range. Multiply each rating by its weight, then add. What are the two totals?
Without applying, what can you learn about each one's loan rules, sample rates and fees?
Who insures your savings at each one? Name the insurer and the limit, and say where you confirmed it.
Will you choose a bank, a credit union or a hybrid? Name your first step and the date you will review.
